messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Amina is a 43-year-old married woman who works in IT support for a mid-sized company, and when she first began speaking about why she had come to treatment, she did so hesitantly, as if even putting words to it might pull her somewhere she did not want to go. She grew up with a caregiver who was physically abusive, and one of the memories that has remained most sharply with her is of being dragged into a small storage shed behind the house after being accused of “causing trouble.” She remembers the smell of damp earth and cut grass outside, the dimness once the door shut, and the feeling of having nowhere to move while blows came. The setting itself became part of the terror: the pressed-in air of a locked space, the sound of the latch, and beyond that the ordinary calm of trees and dirt that now feels to her like a betrayal. Even now, talking about those moments can feel less like telling a story than stepping back into it.

Over the years, Amina came to believe that what happened said something essential about her. She had not simply been a child harmed by an adult; she had come to believe there was something about her that made it happen, something defective in her character that invited cruelty. When she tries to explain this, she says it with a kind of weary certainty: other children must have had something solid in them that she lacked. Those beliefs do not stay abstract. They seem to keep her body braced, as if it is preparing for the next exposure of whatever is wrong with her. She lives with a near-constant tension in her shoulders and chest, and at work she often finds herself rereading the same support ticket because her attention splinters so quickly. A dropped object in the office or a door closing somewhere down the hall can make her jolt before she has time to think, reacting as though danger is already present.

Those same beliefs also shape what catches her. Being asked directly about her childhood in conversation can make her stomach drop, because speaking of the abuse feels like confirming the sort of person she fears herself to be. A locked conference room during a troubleshooting meeting can suddenly feel intolerable, not only because of the enclosed space itself but because it stirs the old conviction that she is once again trapped in something meant for her. Even family outings that should be relaxing have become difficult. If her husband suggests a walk on a wooded trail or a picnic in a park, Amina notices the smell of soil and greenery almost immediately, and with it comes the sense that she is back near the shed, back in a place where bad things happen because of who she is.

Once her body has gone on alert, it seems to deepen the same harsh conclusions about herself. She notices how quickly she startles, how hard it is to focus, how often she reacts before she can judge whether anything is actually wrong, and she reads these responses as further proof that there is something wrong with her as a person. In her mind, a normal person would be able to sit in a room with the door closed, discuss difficult history, or walk through a natural setting without coming apart inside. Each false alarm becomes evidence. The more keyed up she feels, the more defective she believes herself to be, and that belief makes the next surge of tension easier to ignite.

Her sense of danger also narrows her world in concrete ways. In the IT department, she has started avoiding the small back server room unless someone else is with her, even though part of her job is to troubleshoot equipment there. If a manager wants to shut the door to talk through a problem, she subtly shifts to keep it cracked open or finds an excuse to step out. During team meetings, if conversation turns personal and someone asks about her childhood or family, her mind goes blank and her body tightens so fast that she can barely track what is being said next. Outdoors, she scans automatically, her muscles set and her attention pulled toward escape routes, until the trees and enclosed paths begin to feel charged. By the time she reacts, she is often already convinced that the place itself is unsafe.

What finally brought Amina to seek help was not one dramatic episode but the accumulation of these moments. Her husband had begun to notice how often she refused weekend plans, and at work she was worried that her concentration was slipping enough for others to see it. More unsettling to her was the feeling that her world was organizing itself around tension, startle, and the need to stay away from anything that might set her off. She came in frightened that if she keeps living this way, she will only confirm what she has long believed about herself. At the same time, she is quietly hoping for the possibility that talking about what happened might not always feel like being trapped inside it again.
